rv.q: The musical's first act is stunningly close to perfect, the other two less fully accomplished.

It’s been over three years since Lincoln Center’s ambitious and winning revival of Thornton Wilder’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play of apocalypse-meets-absurdity The Skin of Our Teeth, which originally premiered on Broadway—mid-World War II—in 1942. Now the Public Theater is mounting Ethan Lipton’s kno...
With the utmost humility, hilarity, and confidence, his only wish is to pull up a chair for a chat with the source material—one apocalyptic era to another.
Survival, like theatregoing, can be exhausting — but we keep showing up, by the seat of our pants.
The Seat of Our Pants, Ethan Lipton's musical adaptation of Thornton Wilder's The Skin of Our Teeth, is both pleasant and entertaining.
It's spruced up and better decorated, but the bones haven't been touched.
Act I contains every strength, theme, and comic outtake of the overall production and runs just under one hour...I'd have been quite content to see the evening end there.

I witnessed the premiere of The Seat of Our Pants at The Public Theater, and found the show to be pretty much a dud both as a musical and a production, only sporadically brightened by lively performances.
According to the program notes, The Seat of Our Pants has been in development for ten years; the figure is alarming because -- there's no other way to say it -- the piece is a total failure.
This musical version delivers something quite exhilarating and moving, filling me with a deep appreciation of the chaos and its containment.
Lipton's genius is recognizing that musicalization shouldn't tame Wilder's chaos—it should add another layer of theatrical self-awareness.
The Seat of Our Pants is not for everyone, but fans of Wilder will rejoice at this fresh take on a genuine classic.
A fantastic cast gamely attempts to justify this musical adaptation, but The Seat of Our Pants never answers why Thornton Wilder's masterpiece needed singing in the first place.

But watching the cast, led by wonderful performances by Grotelueschen (Into the Woods, Pericles) and Diamond (Parade, The Cher Show), having so much fun — even band member Allison Ann Kelly gets in on the action — is infectious.
